newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Argentina misses out in race for Falklands oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Argentina misses out in race for Falklands oil.

text.p: The Falkland Islands authorities on Monday snubbed Buenos Aires by failing to allow Argentina's YPF oil company to drill for oil in waters surrounding the disputed British territory.
YPF, in partnership with British Gas, applied for the right to explore areas north of the islands but came away empty handed when the first oil exploration licences were awarded.
"That was the only consortium that got nothing but that was partly because they limited their bidding to the two most successful tranches," said chief executive of the Falkland Islands Andrew Gurr.
Argentina was quick to play down suggestions of a rift with Britain, saying it saw no hidden political motive behind the recently-privatised YPF's failure to win oil concessions.

"The British government has assured us that the fact that YPF did not get a license responds to purely commercial reasons and that political circumstances did not have any influence," a government official told Reuters in Buenos Aires.

The Falklands oil exploration announcement comes after Britain vehemently denied newspaper reports earlier this month that it had relaxed an arms embargo against Argentina in return for a pledge by Buenos Aires to allow the oil deal to go through without fuss.

Under Monday's agreements, 12 firms will explore about 12,800 square kilometres of waters north of the islands, which saw a 10-week war in 1982 as a British task force ended a brief Argentine occupation.

Despite Buenos Aires' constitutional claim to the islands, Britain and Argentina restored diplomatic links in 1989 and last year signed an agreement on a framework for oil and gas exploration in Falkland waters.
Gurr said he regretted the failure of the British-Argentine bid but stressed the licences were awarded purely on a commercial basis.

"YPF has a low-risk strategy for exploration. Basically, it bid for the two safest, most popular areas and that is the reason they didn't get anything," said Andres Pitchon, analyst at Salomon Brothers in Buenos Aires.

But some industry sources were suprised by the exclusion of the Argentines, particularly as one consortium, led by British independent oil company LASMO, was unusually awarded not one but two of the most attractive tranches that were up for grabs.
"I'm very surprised that they've come away with nothing," said a source familiar with the YPF bid.
"I would have expected them to curry favour with Argentina by giving them either tranche B or C," he added of the most attractive exploraion areas on offer.
British Gas said it was disappointed but would study future opportunities in the region.

A spokesman for Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell, which won a concession with Italy's Agip, said the ban on Argentine citizens landing on the islands would be "slightly inconvenient" but would not prove a significant obstacle to operations.
"This is an opportunity which we feel is worthwhile or we wouldn't have bid. We're very pleased to get a licence," the official said.

Industry analysts said suggestions the Falklands could be sitting on oil wealth to rival the North Sea, which still has 27 billion barrels of recoverable reserves after more than 20 years of production, were wildly exaggerated.

"If you add together all the prospects in the North Falklands Basin you come to a figure of 2 to 3 billion barrels but that doesn't take account of risk," said Neil Anderson of Edinburgh-based Wood MacKenzie Consultants.
The first phase of exploration, which is expected to last about five years, could create 100 jobs in service industries on the sparsely populated islands, Gurr said.

Anderson and others said the lack of infrastructure and the remoteness of the islands would quadruple drilling costs, raising the economic threshold for individual prospects to about 200 million barrels.
And there was less than a one in 10 chance of finding prospects of this size in the areas offered for exploration, Anderson added.
